german: Im November ist es in Deutschland oft neblig.

hints.hint: You may be thinking "cloudy" here but we already know that's wolkig. Think of something else that would make for a grey day.

reveal: November was once called Nebelmond in German, or the "month of fog". As you may have guessed, Nebel ~ "nebula", both originally meaning "mist" or "cloud". But beware the "false friend" Mist, which means "manure" — quite a semantic drift!

german: Im Frühling gibt es viele Blumen.

hints.hint: We've seen viel(e) before in Ich habe zu viel Wein getrunken. 🥂🥴
The singular is Blume. Does it sound like an English word you know?

reveal: Out of the words for 🌸 the oldest English word is "blossom". English then got "bloom" as a borrowing from Old Norse in the Viking invasions of Britain. So English has two cognates of Blume at its disposal. Another conquest - the Normans - brought "flower" from French "fleur" into the language.

german: Im Winter trägt man warme Kleidung.
reveal: Kleidung has not one but two cognates in English — "clothing" and "cladding" (clothing for buildings!). We also retain the verb form "clad" as in "clad in shining armour", but it does sound a little medieval.

german: Magst du sonniges Wetter oder kaltes Wetter?

hints.hint: We saw a different version of this verb before in Ich möchte nicht arbeiten!.

reveal: Personally I'm for sonniges UND kaltes Wetter.

german: Ein Regenmantel ist eine Art Kleidung.

hints.hint: Regenmantel = Regen + Mantel. You know Regen. Mantel ~ "mantle" — a large covering garment.
Art ~ "sort/kind" — as in the archaic English "after this art" meaning "of this kind".

reveal: Mantel ~ "mantle" — as in the mantle of leadership, or the earth's mantle — all from the same root of a large covering garment. And Kleid ~ "clad" ~ "cloak" — there's a whole cluster of covering and clothing words that go back to the same idea of wrapping yourself up against the elements.
